items.title: A mole of marshmallows would cover the USA 600 miles deep
items.claim: 6.022 times 10 to the 23 is just a number until you try to picture it. Avogadro's number of marshmallows would bury the entire surface of the United States to a depth of 600 miles.
items.prompt: Roughly how many moles of water molecules are in a single drop (about 0.05 mL)?

options.text: About 0.003 moles, which is roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules
Around 6 times 10 to the 23 — one drop is one mole
About 0.05 moles, the same as the volume in millilitres

items.reveal_title: Even a microscopic drop contains stupefying numbers of molecules
items.reveal:
0.05 mL of water has a mass of 0.05 g. Water is 18 g per mole, so 0.05 / 18 equals about 0.0028 mol. Multiply by Avogadro's number and you get roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules.

If you counted those molecules at one per second, it would take about 50 trillion years — over 3000 times the age of the universe. Chemistry is the study of mind-bending counts of incredibly tiny things.
items.why: The mole is treated as a unit conversion when it should be treated as a stark statement about scale.

items.title: A buffer works best when pH = pKa — even though that means it's only half-effective
items.claim: A buffer is maximally effective at resisting pH change when [HA] = [A-], which means pH = pKa by Henderson-Hasselbalch. Counter-intuitively, this is when only half the acid is dissociated — not when you've added the most base.
items.prompt: Why does maximum buffering happen at half-neutralisation?

options.text: Because half-neutralisation is the only stable condition
Adding acid converts A- to HA and vice versa; the ratio [HA]/[A-] changes most slowly when the two are equal — small additions barely shift the log of the ratio, so pH barely changes
Buffers cannot work outside pH = pKa
Acid and base cancel only at pKa

items.reveal:
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]).

If [HA] = [A-] (i.e. pH = pKa), then log term = 0 and small changes in [A-] or [HA] barely shift pH. Capacity is maximised within ±1 pH unit of pKa.

Move far from pKa and a buffer collapses: at pH = pKa + 2, [A-]/[HA] = 100; adding more acid takes it from 100 to 50 — only a 0.3 pH change at first, but the conjugate base is rapidly used up.

This is why biological buffers are tuned to the physiological pH they need to defend: phosphate (pKa2 = 7.2) inside cells, carbonate-bicarbonate (open system at pH 7.4) in blood. Choosing pKa to match the target pH is buffer design 101.
items.why: Maximum effectiveness coincides with 'only half the acid is reacted' — a useful surprise that follows directly from the log.

items.title: Mass spec can distinguish CO from N2 — molecules differing by 0.004 atomic mass units
items.claim: Carbon monoxide has exact mass 28.0101 u. Nitrogen gas has exact mass 28.0061 u. A high-resolution mass spectrometer can tell them apart routinely. Modern Orbitrap and FT-ICR instruments achieve resolutions of 1 part in 100,000 or better.

options.text: By weighing on a very sensitive scale

By measuring the frequency at which ions orbit in a magnetic or electrostatic trap; ion frequency is a precise function of mass-to-charge, and modern electronics measure frequencies to extraordinary precision
By averaging millions of low-resolution scans

items.reveal:
In an FT-ICR mass spectrometer, ions trapped in a magnetic field B orbit at the cyclotron frequency f = qB/(2πm). The image current induced in detection plates is recorded and Fourier-transformed to give the mass spectrum.

Frequency can be measured to about 1 part in 10 to the 9; mass-to-charge can be determined to about 1 part in 10 to the 6 with a well-calibrated instrument.

This is why high-resolution mass spec can identify peptides by exact mass alone, distinguish isotope clusters in metabolites, and resolve overlapping signals in complex mixtures. Proteomics, drug metabolism, environmental analysis and forensics all rely on it.

The 0.004 u difference between CO and N2 comes from the slightly different nuclear binding energies of the constituent nuclei — mass spec is sensitive enough to probe nuclear physics from chemistry samples.
items.why: Mass spec sounds like 'a scale for molecules'. It is really a precision frequency measurement of trapped ions in fields.
